directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Blondie produces bright, warm golden-blonde foliage with a slight ruffled texture, one of the brighter and more consistently colored gold heucheras available, holding its warm tone through the season better than many gold cultivars that fade to chartreuse in shade or bleach out in strong sun. In early summer it sends up airy, wiry stems of small white flowers above the foliage that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Frosted Violet Heuchera (Silver-Frosted Purple Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Frosted Violet bears deep purple leaves overlaid with a silvery-white frosted sheen across the upper surface, a metallic, icy effect that shifts and shimmers with changing light, distinguishing it from the many solid-purple heuchera cultivars. Its cool, silvery-purple tone pairs well with pink- and white-flowered shade companions and provides striking contrast against gold hostas or chartreuse foliage. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Timeless Treasure Heuchera (Silver-Overlay Rose-Veined Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Timeless Treasure bears large, ruffled leaves in silvery-rose overlaid on a purple base, with contrasting darker veining that traces each leaf in a lace-like pattern, giving the foliage a rich, layered, almost painted look that holds up well through the growing season. Its bold leaf size and dramatic coloring make it a strong accent plant in shaded containers and border fronts. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Silver Scrolls Heuchera (Silver-Purple Veined Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Silver Scrolls is a longtime favorite heuchera cultivar with large, glossy, silvery-gray leaves traced by bold, dark purple veining that stands out sharply against the pale metallic background, an early and influential introduction in the wave of silver-leaved heucheras that followed. In early summer it sends up tall, wiry stems of small white flowers above the foliage that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Root Beer Heuchera (Ruffled Cinnamon-Bronze Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Root Beer bears large, heavily ruffled leaves in a warm cinnamon-bronze color with a glossy, almost caramel-toned sheen, a distinctive warm tone that stands apart from the more common purple, silver, and gold heuchera palettes. Its bold texture and rich brown-bronze color make it a versatile companion for both warm- and cool-toned shade plantings, pairing especially well with orange- or rust-toned flowers. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Iron Butterfly Tiarella (Deeply Cut Dark-Centered Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; forms a slowly spreading, non-invasive clump.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Iron Butterfly bears finely cut, almost fern-like or butterfly-shaped leaves marked with a bold, dark purple-black central blaze along the veins, a more deeply dissected leaf form than most foamflower cultivars, topped by fluffy spikes of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers in spring. Its fine texture and dark central marking make it a strong textural contrast to broader-leaved hostas and heucheras in a shaded planting, and foliage often takes on additional burgundy tones through fall, remaining semi-evergreen in milder climates. Divide congested clumps in spring or fall every few years to maintain vigor.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Candy Striper produces maple-like green leaves marked by a bold, dark burgundy central blaze, topped in spring by dense spikes of flowers that open a distinctive candy-pink and fade paler as they age, a stronger pink flower color than the white or pale pink typical of most foamflower cultivars. It forms a dense, slowly spreading, non-aggressive clump ideal for the front of a shaded border or massed as a groundcover beneath deciduous trees. Divide congested clumps in spring or fall every few years to maintain vigor, and combine with hosta, heuchera, and ferns for season-long foliage and flower contrast.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; tolerates dry shade under trees once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Amber Queen produces sprays of warm amber-orange flowers with a coppery cast in spring, an unusual warm tone distinct from the more common yellow, white, and pink epimedium flower colors, held above heart-shaped leaves that emerge bronze-tinted and mature to green. Its clump-forming habit spreads gradually into a dense, weed-suppressing patch useful for underplanting trees and shrubs in a woodland garden. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Pink Champagne bears large, mottled foliage speckled with maroon spots over green, particularly striking as new growth emerges in spring, paired with dainty sprays of pink-and-white spurred flowers held above the leaves. Its patterned foliage provides ornamental interest well beyond the relatively brief spring bloom period, making it a strong textural and color accent for a shaded border or woodland planting. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring display.

common_name: Cherry Hearts Epimedium (Heart-Shaped Leaf Cherry-Red Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Cherry Hearts is named for its distinctly heart-shaped leaflets, which emerge tinged in red-bronze in spring before maturing to green, paired with sprays of bright cherry-red flowers with white-tipped spurs held on wiry stems above the foliage. Its compact size and distinctive leaf shape make it a good choice for the front of a shaded border or a woodland rock garden where its detail can be appreciated up close. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring display.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Spine Tingler bears glossy, evergreen leaves edged in fine, prickly spines, a distinctly bold, holly-like texture unlike the smooth-margined foliage of most epimedium cultivars, topped in spring by sprays of pale yellow flowers with a delicate, spurred form. Its spiny-edged, deer-resistant foliage provides year-round textural interest in a shaded border or woodland garden even outside the spring bloom season. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring display.

common_name: Visions in Red Astilbe (Deep Red Compact Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; more tolerant of drier soil and sun than most astilbe cultivars, though consistent moisture gives the best results.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Visions in Red produces dense, bottlebrush-like plumes in a deep, saturated wine-red, a richer and darker color than the raspberry-pink of the original Visions astilbe, above glossy, dark bronze-green, finely cut foliage that adds color contrast even before bloom. Like other Astilbe chinensis selections, it tolerates somewhat drier soil and more sun than Arendsii-type astilbes, though it still performs best with consistent moisture and appreciates deep shade and heavy mulch through the hottest part of a zone 9 summer. The dried flower plumes remain attractive well after bloom; divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Delft Lace Astilbe (Bronze Foliage Pale-Pink Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Delft Lace is grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, with deeply cut, glossy leaves that emerge bronze-purple in spring and hold noticeable dark tinting through the season, setting off airy, feathery plumes of soft pale pink flowers in mid-summer. Its distinctive dark foliage adds ornamental interest before and after the bloom period, unlike many astilbe cultivars valued for flowers alone. Consistent moisture is essential — astilbes wilt and scorch quickly in dry shade; divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor, and mulch well to conserve soil moisture through summer heat.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun. Color Flash is grown primarily for its unusual foliage, which shifts through the season from green to purple to burgundy-red as summer progresses, an ongoing color transition that few other astilbe cultivars offer, topped by soft pink flower plumes in summer that are almost secondary to the changing leaf color. Its dynamic, ever-shifting foliage provides months of interest beyond the relatively brief flowering period typical of most astilbes. Consistent moisture is essential — astilbes wilt and scorch quickly in dry shade; divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor, and mulch well to conserve soil moisture through summer heat.
